video.title: Why This Olympic Sport Bothers Physicists

protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output or other labels.
protocol.times_from: Lemonfox transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: Curling etiquette: players tally their own points and call their own fouls even at the Olympics, always shake hands, must compliment each other's shots, and the winners buy the first round of beers (167.6, the punchline). Tightest cut is ~20s, under the band; nothing before it adds to it.

Surprising fact: every Olympic curling stone comes from one Scottish company and one island, a 60-million-year-old granite plug low in aluminum, giving a tight structure that makes the stones water- and crack-resistant (233.7). The price kicker ($600 a stone, $9,600 a set, 241.1) is an acceptable longer end.

Explanation: curling is the only Olympic sport where players manipulate the object after it's thrown -- by changing the ice. The ice is deliberately pebbled; sweeping melts the pebbles into a thin water film, so the stone slides up to three meters farther. Hook is the 'only Olympic sport' line (362.6 'But this is actually very unique' points back).

Story: in 2015 a directional-fabric broom got too effective; players turned pads inside out as a courtesy, then a coarser broom let sweepers steer the stone like a joystick; 22 teams agreed not to use them though no rule existed, and within a year the federation made them illegal (579.9). Ending on the teams' voluntary pact (571.8) also lands. Opening on the news clips ('performance-enhancing brooms', 497.4) is a stronger hook but runs to ~82s.

Physics mystery: a curling stone curls the same direction it spins; a spinning glass curls the opposite way because the front has more friction -- normal, expected -- 'curling stones do the opposite', and we've been asking why for a hundred years (665.6). Hook 'the stone curls in the same direction that it spins'.

Hot take plus joke: curling isn't new, it's 'the most Olympic sport, and I will die on this pebbled, icy hill' -- in the first Winter Olympics in 1924, maybe one of the oldest team sports; a stone from a bog dated 1511 means Da Vinci could have met his curling league after painting the Mona Lisa (punchline, 703.8).

Why the curling puzzle matters: missions to icy moons with oceans underneath need robots that drill or melt through 30 km of ice, and how a spinning robot interacts with the ice is the same physics problem as curling -- 'it's all connected' (787.3). Preferred opens on 'Finding alien life, seriously' (after 'And my favorite example'); opening at 709.7 ('it's not just about this game ... tribology') gives the setup but runs ~78s. Both edges genuinely work.

Closing take: why it frustrates her when people mock curling -- it's lame to be the constant cynic, you only see the surface; dig deeper and the strange thing turns out most interesting; 'you just have to be willing to turn over those stones' (955.1).

also_ok.why: Viewer tip: sweeping also scratches the ice and steers the curl; two sweepers means they want distance, one sweeper means they're steering. Useful but leans on the sweeping explanation before it.

negatives.why: Intro trailer: 'tech doping scandal', 'physics mystery unsolved for a century' -- teases with no payoff here.
Her failed throws, 'Nope, nope, nope' -- room/on-screen moment.
Draw/takeout/guard strategy and 'best shot I've ever seen in my life' -- narration of play on screen.
'How do you know which one's the skip? He's the one yelling his head off' -- a laugh that needs the footage.
Theories 'totally wrong' and 'didn't work' -- depend on the glass-friction setup and each other.
